nameStory: The Concentric Ring Lichen gets its name from its distinctive growth pattern that creates perfect circles expanding outward from the center, like ripples in a pond. As this lichen grows slowly over many years, it spreads in all directions equally, forming these remarkable ring patterns that can be spotted from quite a distance. The scientific name 'centrifuga' literally means 'fleeing from the center,' perfectly describing how it grows outward in concentric circles.
description: Concentric Ring Lichen is a shield lichen that forms striking circular patches on rocks and stone surfaces. It belongs to the ring lichen family, creating distinctive target-like patterns as it grows slowly outward from a central point. These circular colonies can expand over many decades, with the outer edges being the youngest, most active growth. The lichen has a foliose (leaf-like) growth form that lies relatively flat against its rocky home.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms perfect or near-perfect concentric circles on rock surfaces, like natural bull's-eyes that can be several inches to over a foot across

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found exclusively on hard rock surfaces, particularly favoring granite, quartzite, and other acidic stone substrates

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels papery and somewhat brittle when dry, with a slightly wrinkled surface that becomes more pliable when moist

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual rings can range from a few inches to over 12 inches in diameter, with older specimens forming the largest, most perfect circles

habitat: Look for Concentric Ring Lichen on exposed rock faces, boulder fields, and stone outcrops throughout New England's mountains and hills. It particularly favors acidic rocks like granite and quartzite in areas with good air circulation and moderate moisture. You'll often find it on south-facing rock surfaces that get plenty of light but aren't constantly wet.

seasonality.spring: Spring rains bring out the vibrant green colors as the lichen absorbs moisture and becomes more photosynthetically active. The concentric ring pattern is most obvious when wet.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, the lichen appears grayish and papery, with the ring patterns still visible but less dramatic in color contrast.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture from rain and fog revives the green coloration, making this an excellent time to spot the distinctive circular growth patterns.
seasonality.winter: Snow may cover specimens, but when visible, winter lichens appear muted in color while maintaining their characteristic ring structure underneath ice and snow.

funFact: Some Concentric Ring Lichen colonies are estimated to be hundreds of years old, growing outward at a rate of just millimeters per year - meaning that large rings you see today may have started growing before the American Revolution!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other circular-growing lichens or even fairy rings of moss, but the perfect concentric pattern and exclusive growth on hard rock (never soil) makes it distinctive. Remember: if it's a perfect circle on stone, it's likely this species.
contextualKnowledge: Ring lichens like this one are sometimes called 'compass lichens' by hikers because they often grow most vigorously on the side facing away from prevailing winds, though this isn't reliable enough for actual navigation.
compareHints: Concentric Ring Lichen differs from its relative, Finger Ring Lichen, by forming complete, unbroken circles rather than incomplete or finger-like projections. While Finger Ring Lichen may have gaps or irregular edges in its growth pattern, Concentric Ring Lichen maintains its perfect circular form. Both grow on rock, but only Concentric Ring Lichen creates those distinctive bull's-eye patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Finger Ring Lichen differs from its close relative Concentric Ring Lichen by having much narrower, more tightly curved lobes that create more intricate ring patterns.
